title: That they all may be one (John 17:20–23)
word: That they all may be one
hook: his prayer for unity, the charter of Christian unity work

segments.voice: Yesterday, sorrow turned into joy, like labor into birth. Your line was your joy no man shall take. What small joy did you keep? Day five hundred twenty-five.

On a single street in many towns you can find a Catholic parish, a Baptist church, a Greek Orthodox church and a Lutheran one, each with its own sign out front. Every Sunday they read from the same Gospels. Christians have been divided for a long time, some of the splits nearly a thousand years old, some five hundred, some newer. So it's striking to remember that, in John's Gospel, the last thing Jesus does before he walks out to the garden is pray out loud. And part of what he prays for is the people on that street.
screen: `FOUR CHURCHES, ONE STREET.` → `SPLITS CENTURIES OLD.` → `THE LAST THING HE DOES: PRAY.`

segments.voice: John seventeen is sometimes called the high priestly prayer. Jesus lifts his eyes to heaven and prays for himself, then for the disciples at the table. Then he looks further: not for them only, but for those who will believe in me through their word. That's everyone after them. And here's what he asks, in the Douay-Rheims: "That they all may be one, as thou, Father, in me, and I in thee; that they also may be one in us; that the world may believe that thou hast sent me." Notice the measure, again. Not one the way a club is one, or a company. One as the Father and the Son are one. And notice the reason: that the world may believe. Unity isn't a private comfort. It's a sign, the same way the new commandment was a sign. Catholics call efforts toward Christian unity ecumenism, and they point to this prayer as its charter. In 1964 the Second Vatican Council issued a decree on ecumenism, saying that division openly contradicts the will of Christ. In 1995 Pope John Paul the Second wrote a whole letter on Christian unity, and gave it this prayer's Latin as its title: Ut unum sint, that they may be one. Every January, from the eighteenth to the twenty-fifth, Catholics, Orthodox and Protestant Christians in many places keep a Week of Prayer for Christian Unity together. That's week seventy-five: my peace I give, the vine, greater love, friends, the Spirit of truth, sorrow into joy, and now, that they may be one.
screen: `THE HIGH PRIESTLY PRAYER.` · `FOR THOSE WHO WILL BELIEVE.` · `ONE AS THE FATHER AND SON.` · `UT UNUM SINT, 1995.` · then, large: `THAT THEY ALL MAY BE ONE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hold the divided church. Sit, and breathe. Picture the churches near you, not just your own, all of them, the buildings and the people inside. Picture someone you love who worships somewhere different, or who stopped going. Don't argue anything in your head. Just hold them all together, side by side. If you pray, you can pray Jesus's own words for them, that they all may be one. If you don't, simply hold the picture of them gathered in one place. The bell holds the time.
That they all may be one. Jesus's prayer the night before he died, for all who would believe, that their unity would be a sign to the world. Today's word.
screen: `THAT THEY ALL MAY BE ONE — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: that they may be one. Today, say something kind and true about a church that isn't yours. Day five hundred twenty-five.

original.note: Greek: that they all may be one (John 17:21). Latin: ut omnes unum sint.

trapdoor: what you thought: a wish that Christians would get along.
what it means: a prayer for a unity modeled on the Father and Son, meant as a sign so the world may believe.
what a scholar hears: the label 'high priestly prayer' is usually traced to the Lutheran theologian David Chytraeus in the 1500s; the Latin gave John Paul II's 1995 encyclical its name.
